subject: history
title: Industrial Revolution and Urbanisation
welcome_lead: Steam, factories and the transformation of British society from 1750 to 1900.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on the Industrial Revolution, urbanisation and reform.
final_note: You have heard the looms and the chartist crowds.

concepts.def: Transformation c. 1750-1900 from agrarian to industrial economy, powered by coal, steam and factory production.
Conversion of common land into privately held fields, accelerating after 1760 via parliamentary Acts.
Multi-spindle machine invented by James Hargreaves c. 1764, revolutionising cotton production.
Mass migration to cities; Manchester grew from c. 25,000 in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1851.
1832 statute extending the franchise to middle-class men and redistributing seats.
Working-class movement 1838-58 demanding the Six Points of the People's Charter, including universal male suffrage.

walkthroughs.body_html: Britain combined abundant coal, navigable waterways, agricultural improvement freeing labour, colonial markets, scientific culture and a stable legal order protecting property. Watt's separate-condenser steam engine of 1769 multiplied power. Inventions in textiles (Arkwright's water frame 1769, Crompton's mule 1779) created factory production. By 1851 the Great Exhibition celebrated British industrial primacy.

Cities grew faster than infrastructure. Cholera epidemics in 1832 and 1848 spurred Chadwick's 1842 Sanitary Report and the 1848 Public Health Act. Working hours in factories were limited by the 1833 Factory Act (no children under 9 in textiles) and the 1847 Ten Hours Act. Trade unions, legalised in 1824, expanded after 1871, reshaping working-class politics.

The 1832 Great Reform Act enfranchised middle-class male householders worth GBP 10 and abolished rotten boroughs. The 1867 Reform Act doubled the electorate to two million, including urban workers. The 1884 Act extended county franchise. Chartism (1838-58) failed in 1848 but most of its six points were eventually adopted, completing parliamentary democracy by 1928.

mcqs.q: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
options: Because Britain banned slavery before other countries.
William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
A combination of capital from trade and empire, coal and iron deposits, agricultural improvements, political stability, and a culture of invention.
Because James Watt invented the steam engine.

mcqs.q: Why did Chartism fail in the short term?
options: Chartism failed because Queen Victoria personally banned the movement.
Because Britain banned slavery before other countries.
Chartism failed because no one supported it.
Mass petitions were rejected by Parliament; the movement split between moral-force and physical-force wings; economic improvement after 1848 reduced support.
